name: Memberstack
tagline: Authentication, gated content, subscriptions, and member data for websites

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Build Mode
tiers.limits: Free until launch; no card required; 0 production/live-site allowance published.

tiers.name: Basic
tiers.limits: Up to 1,000 members; 4% Memberstack transaction fee.

tiers.name: Professional
tiers.limits: Up to 5,000 members; 2% Memberstack transaction fee.

tiers.name: 200 Member Plan
tiers.limits: Up to 200 members and 0% Memberstack transaction fee.
tiers.notes: Specialty plan for productized-service businesses; monthly price only.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Build Mode is free until launch but is not a production plan; no numeric live-member allowance is published
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual for core plans; 200 Member Plan is monthly; 30-day money-back guarantee
pricing.hiddenCosts: Basic/Professional/Business add 4%/2%/0.9% platform fees on top of Stripe processing; crossing member limits requires a higher plan.

verdictSummary: The visible website memberships loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Memberstack earns its keep through payments, network, compliance, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a narrow website memberships storefront or member area for one creator, using Stripe Checkout and explicit digital-delivery rules.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: Stripe account and API keys in .env
whatYouLose: tax, disputes, payouts, and fraud operations
whyPeopleStillPay: Memberstack: Creators pay to outsource payments, tax complexity, disputes, deliverability, moderation, and the trust needed to convert strangers.
ongoingBurden: Own payments, webhooks, refunds, tax records, fraud, access control, file delivery, moderation, backups, and support.

alternatives.name: Ghost
alternatives.desc: All four nouns are present, but the website becomes a Ghost publication rather than keeping its current stack.

facts.install: Run Ghost-CLI on supported Ubuntu/MySQL hosting; the official Docker path is available but still documented as preview
facts.dataFormat: Posts, members and settings in MySQL; images under Ghost's content directory by default or through a configured storage adapter
facts.gapVsPaid: Ghost cannot attach auth, member records and billing to an arbitrary existing stack; the site becomes a Ghost publication.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting needs a server, domain, DNS, TLS and transactional/newsletter mail, plus Ghost upgrades

alternatives.name: Paid Memberships Pro
alternatives.desc: Authentication, member records, recurring billing and gated content inside WordPress; arbitrary-site embedding is gone.

facts.install: Install the WordPress plugin, create membership levels/pages, then connect a supported payment gateway
facts.dataFormat: WordPress users/usermeta plus PMPro membership, order and discount tables; card credentials remain with the payment gateway
facts.gapVsPaid: Paid Memberships Pro works inside WordPress rather than embedding cleanly into arbitrary Webflow, React or custom sites.
facts.setupBlocker: A maintained WordPress/HTTPS site, payment gateway, webhooks and reliable email delivery are prerequisites

alternatives.name: systeme.io
alternatives.desc: Hosted users, subscriptions and gated content for a small membership site; you move the site into its ecosystem.

facts.dataFormat: Contacts, funnels, course/community content, orders, emails and uploaded files in systeme.io's vendor-managed cloud; the underlying storage format is not published
facts.gapVsPaid: systeme.io cannot drop authentication and billing into an arbitrary existing site the way Memberstack can; the site moves into systeme.io.
facts.setupBlocker: Selling requires connecting a payment gateway; the free plan is capped at 2,000 contacts, three funnels, one course, one community and one custom domain

rejectedAlternatives.name: Medusa
rejectedAlternatives.desc: It handles commerce primitives, not drop-in site authentication, member data and content gating.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Supabase
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Auth and data are there, but this is a developer backend, not a membership product a non-builder installs.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Memberstack is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Memberstack, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + PostgreSQL + Stripe.
Primary job: Build a narrow website memberships storefront or member area for one creator, using Stripe Checkout and explicit digital-delivery rules.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: native apps and community moderation; fulfilment, email, and affiliate ecosystems; marketplace discovery and buyer trust.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
